sentence: The sources reviewed here offer several mechanisms by which stated goals can diverge from the goals that actually govern a person's satisfaction, persistence, and eventual judgment of success: action identification theory [Vallacher & Wegner, Psychological Review, 1987], goal systems theory [Kruglanski, New Developments in Goal Systems Theory, OUP, 2023], self-concordance research [Sheldon & Elliot, JPSP, 1999], conversation-analytic work on presupposition [Schoeb, Studies in Communication Sciences, 2014], and an engineering folklore tradition (the XY problem) that arrived at a similar descrip

The canonical worked example is the filename-extension dialogue: the asker requests the last three characters of a filename when the underlying need is the file extension, which three characters do not reliably capture [xyproblem.info, n.d.].

**Markers.** Practitioners converge on recognizable surface features: questions opening "How can I…" are treated as "almost like a red flag" provoking the counter-question "What's your use-case?" [Dodds, tkdodo.eu, 2021]; questions consisting mostly of what was tried rather than why the task exists in the first place [expo/fyi, "Don't ask about solutions

The only quantitative-sounding claim is Batchelder's report that knowing the underlying reason changes his answer "75% of the time": an explicit practitioner self-estimate, not a measured rate [Batchelder, 2013].

Any number attached to "how common is the XY problem" is currently unsupported.

**Causes as practitioners see them.** The folklore offers multiple, not mutually exclusive, mechanisms: getting "stuck on what they believe is the solution" and unable to step back [xyproblem.info]; working forward from problem to solution and asking about the point of sticking [Batchelder, 2013]; deliberately asking a narrow question "to not take up too much of the helper's time" [Batchelder, 2013]; and, inside organizations, junior engineers assuming all solutions were already chosen for them ("solution blinders

The claim that stigma and impression management systematically distort *stated goals* in help-seeking is plausible and pointed to by retrieved titles, but is unverified in this corpus.

## 1.5 What this section could not support

- Any prevalence rate for the XY problem, in any corpus (only the flagged practitioner estimate exists) [Batchelder, 2013].
- Direct Nisbett–Wilson-lineage findings on introspective access to the causes of one's own behavior (present only as citations inside other sources).
- Test-retest stability (or instability) of laddering-derived value hierarchies: posed by the c
The training literature warns that MI strategies used without the spirit are ineffective, a claim the founders assert rather than demonstrate [Lubman et al., 2012].
The basic skills are the OARS quartet: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries [Lubman et al., 2012].

The guiding principles are compressed into RULE, and the first letter is the theory of why stated goals mislead: Resist the righting reflex (elsewhere in this report also called the advice-giving reflex; the terms are synonyms) [Lubman et al., 2012].

The focusing process is MI's explicit machinery for goal selection: identifying candidate topics, prioritising one from many (the "agenda mapping" strategy), then holding the conversation on the agreed focus so change talk in that area can be recognised and reinforced [Gobat et al., 2018].

Gobat and colleagues also note that institutional agendas often only partially map onto the change conversation the client is ready to have, so the focus itself must be negotiated, not assumed [Gobat et al., 2018].

The signature question moves are open questions that evoke the client's own reasons ("What concerns do you have about your drinking?" rather than "Are you concerned about your drinking?"), reflections that differentially strengthen change talk, and explicit linkage of the behaviour to the client's values and future goals [Lubman et al., 2012].

The signature moves are staged open questions: goal ("what do you want?"), reality ("what is happening now?"), option-generation, and will/commitment questions, applied flexibly rather than strictly in sequence [Panchal & Riddell, 2020].

The GROWS proposal grafts obstacle-anticipation and relapse-recovery questions from the Health Action Process Approach onto GROW's Will stage; its supporting study is a pilot with four coaching clients [Panchal & Riddell, 2020].

Beyond that, the evidence is coachee-experience studies [Linder-Pelz & Lawley, International Coaching Psychology Review, 2015], applied case reports (midwifery decision-making, novice teachers), and the explicitly exploratory cognitive-task-analysis proposal [Small & Ey, 2024].

Its theory of misleading goals is that stated preferences sit at the bottom of a hierarchy the respondent has never examined; only probing reveals which values the consequences serve [Reynolds & Gutman, 1988].

The manual is explicit about the interpersonal engineering required: position the respondent as the expert, and even create "a slight sense of vulnerability on the part of the interviewer" to license introspection [Reynolds & Gutman, 1988].

Ulwick's explicit anti-move parallels the XY prescription: never ask "how would you improve this product?"; ask instead what makes the job inconvenient, time-consuming, unstable, or wasteful [Ulwick, 2016].
FLAG: the often-quoted estimate that knowing the underlying reason changes the answer "75% of the time" is one engineer's self-report, not a measured rate [Batchelder, 2013].

On stakeholder goal modelling: formal goal-oriented frameworks (KAOS, i*) appear in the corpus only as passing mentions in technique inventories [Palomares et al., 2021]; the corpus contains no primary empirical study of goal-model-driven elicitation, so no effectiveness claims are made here.

The strongest empirical statements in this lineage are negative or cautionary: Five Whys' single-pathway failure [Card, 2017], laddering's analysis-dependence [Kilwinger & van Dam, 2021], and one trial family in which a scripted GROW chatbot matched the tested human coaching condition on goal attainment [Terblanche et al., 2022], a parity result for that implementation rather than proof that the method in general is mechanizable.
The elevator example, as noted above, is an anecdote appearing "in virtually every design thinking curriculum" [si-labs.com, 2026], not a documented case with measured outcomes.
The "look for positive exceptions" reframing strategy [Wedell-Wedellsborg, 2020] is explicitly borrowed from this solution-focused tradition (the book's index credits Steve de Shazer).

Net: opportunity framing has one supportive RCT on immediate affect and action-step concreteness [Neipp et al., 2021], plus tradition-level endorsement; deficit framing is nowhere shown to be categorically harmful.

## 4.6 Goal decomposition and subgoaling

<!-- editorial:background -->
Goal-systems theory supplies the structural vocabulary for decomposition: goals sit in hierarchies, cognitively linked to means below them; a means may serve a subgoal, which serves an overarching goal.

Two implications for decomposition, both theoretical design risks rather than demonstrated harms of elicitation: goal-systems theory's "more is less" finding (adding alternative means dilutes motivation toward any single means [Kruglanski, Goal Systems Theory volume, 2023]) and the model's warning that prying an intrinsically motivating activity apart into means and separate ends may undermine the experience rather than clarify it [Woolley & Fishbach, 2023].

And self-generated plans, the realistic deployment mode for any dialogue tool, can be built on poorly chosen obstacles or ineffective if-then responses, a quality risk the meta-analysts flag explicitly [Wang & Gai, 2021].

Read together with §4.6's subgoal and planning evidence, a design hypothesis rather than a validated rule, assembled from evidence domains as different as child mathematics learning, implementation-intention meta-analyses, and a theoretical fusion model: decompose for *attainment* when the goal is extrinsic, distal, and stalled (where proximal subgoals and if-then plans have their strongest record [Bandura & Schunk, 1981; Webb & Sheeran, 2007]); avoid or delay decomposition when the pursuit is intrinsically motivated and activity-end fusion may be doing the motivational work [Woolley & Fishbac

At the package level, SFBT meta-analyses disagree on magnitude: early pooling found small effects (d = 0.13–0.26, significant only for internalizing problems) [Kim, Research on Social Work Practice, 2008], while a recent meta of community-based RCTs reports a medium pooled g = 0.654 across 28 studies and 340 effect sizes [Franklin et al., Research on Social Work Practice, 2024]. [disputed: SFBT effect size ranges from ~0.13 to ~0.65 depending on inclusion criteria and comparator type; treat any single figure with caution.]

For dialogue design the transfer claim is direct but, again, untested in conversation: an elicitor's first hypothesis about the user's goal will bias which follow-up questions get asked and which answers get attended to, and merely instructing the elicitor to stay open is exactly the debiasing move that failed in both the interviewing [Rivard, 2014] and Einstellung [Bilalić et al., 2010] literatures.

**Question-behavior / mere-measurement effects.** Corpus coverage here is thin, and this section says so rather than padding.

First, in the one randomized question-type comparison, scaling questions produced more concrete action steps where miracle/exception questions shifted affect [Neipp et al., 2021]; no source in this corpus documents practitioners actually using that contrast as a transition rule, so treating it as a pivot from exploring to planning is a design inference, not an observed practice.

In the one observational sample available, nine experienced therapists' early sessions, "done" looked less like a state of the goal statement than a state of the relationship: the client is engaged, the work feels meaningful, and ambivalence is on the table rather than resolved [Oddli & McLeod, 2014].

Experiential engagement beats rationale-giving in values work [Levin et al., Behavior Therapy, 2012]. **Design inference** (from Oddli & McLeod 2014, Neipp et al. 2021): sequence the dialogue as reflect/validate → evocative probe → (only if the goal frame itself is failing) lateral reframe; select question type by the product needed at that moment, affect shift versus concrete next step, rather than by school loyalty. **Design inference** (from Card's Five Whys critique [BMJ Quality & Safety, 2017] and Dorst's frame-creation method [MIT Press, 2015]): when probing stalls, prefer lateral frame

This is directly implementable: an LLM can be its own cleanness scorer, and no source in the corpus has tested the combination. **Design inference** (from Rivard 2014): when the agent has formed a strong prior about the user's "real" goal, that is precisely when its questions need the strictest cleanness screening, because informed questioners demonstrably contaminate elicitation.

**3.4 Sustain-talk-style back-off signals.** Client language *against* change, not language for it, carries the outcome signal (sustain talk → worse outcome, r = −.24 in the first meta-analysis; independently predic

The Motivation-Aware Framework (CHI 2026) already demonstrates the enabling capability: real-time MI-coding of user utterances into change/sustain expressions with commitment strength, used to route strategy [Motivation-Aware Framework, CHI 2026]. **Design inference** (from Magill 2018 plus the Motivation-Aware Framework (CHI 2026) routing demonstration): treat rising sustain-talk proportion as the agent's primary back-off trigger, shifting from probing to reflection or explicitly offering to drop the thread.

The Motivation-Aware Framework trial (CHI 2026) offers the nearest evidence: routing action-ready users into planning improved perceived planning effectiveness, and plan *agreement* marked the best motivational outcomes [Motivation-Aware Framework, CHI 2026]. **Design inference** (from RegretBench, Gobat et al. 2018, Motivation-Aware Framework CHI 2026): implement the transition as an explicit, user-visible move (a candidate-goal summary offered for confirmation, agenda-mapping style) triggered by the conjunction of low model uncertainty over the goal and low sustain talk, with a hard turn cei

Once past the transition, switch toolkits: implementation-intention and mental-contrasting structures carry the planning-phase evidence (MCII g = 0.336, stronger delivered interactively) [Wang & Gai, Frontiers in Psychology, 2021], with the caveat that subgoal framing as progress rather than commitment can demotivate [Fishbach, Dhar & Zhang, 2006].

**3.6 Flexible policy over rigid script.** MI produced *larger* effects when practiced without a manual [Hettema, Steele & Miller, Annual Review of Clinical Psychology, 2005], and the scripted-GROW parity result is explicitly read by its authors as

The Motivation-Aware Framework (CHI 2026) finding that plan agreement predicted the largest intrinsic-motivation gains is convergent trial-side evidence that the user's endorsement of the selected direction matters [Motivation-Aware Framework, CHI 2026]. **Design inference** (from Sheldon, Prentice & Osin 2019): before locking a goal, the agent should elicit several candidate formulations and probe each for autonomous motivation ("would you still want this if no one ever knew?"), turning a questionnaire manipulation into a dialogue stage.

First, no trial dismantles the *clarification* component from accountability/monitoring components in the successful chatbot RCTs; the one chatbot component trial available in this corpus found the follow-up component, not the MI dialogue, carried the primary outcome [Fitzsimmons-Craft et al., 2024].

Second, safety evidence for prolonged automated probing of values and deeper wants is thin: the trials report harm mitigation in outputs [Meyer & Elsweiler, 2025] and no serious adverse events reported [Wong et al., 2026], which is not the same thing as demonstrated safety, and the corpus contains no study of rumination, destabilized commitments, or dropout caused by deep goal-probing at scale [as of: 2026-08].
